games.title: One for You, One for Me
games.goal: Build one-to-one giving inside a daily routine, no prep
materials: any small items you are already handing out
script: At snack, laundry, or cleanup, hand things out one at a time.
Say the ritual out loud, slowly: "One for you... one for me."
Tap each item as you say its word. The tap is the whole trick.
Sometimes pause with the item in the air and let {name} say the next part.
If {name} grabs a handful, that's fine. Say: "So many!" and keep going.
End before {name} is done wanting it.
games.level_up: Ask once, playfully: "Can you give the bear just one?" Then back to the ritual either way.
games.level_down: Drop the words and keep the rhythm: hand, tap, smile. The pattern comes first.
games.bilingual_note: Use whichever language the routine already happens in. Both work.

games.title: Count the Stairs
games.goal: Attach number words to a body rhythm the child already loves
script: Every time you climb stairs together, count each step out loud: "One, two, three..."
Land the word exactly when a foot lands. The timing does the teaching.
Same stairs, same words, every trip. Toddlers love the sameness.
After a while, pause on a step and wait. Let {name} shout the next word.
Wrong word? Just keep climbing and counting. No fixing.
games.level_up: Start the count at the bottom with a question: "Ready? What comes first?"
games.level_down: Count only the first three steps, big and cheerful, and let the rest be climbing.
games.bilingual_note: Count the same stairs in both home languages on different trips. The rhythm carries over.

games.title: Finger-Tag Number Songs
games.goal: Turn number songs into touch: one word, one finger, every time
script: Pick any counting song you both like. Five little ducks, five little monkeys, anything.
As you sing each number, tap one of {name}'s fingers. One word, one tap.
Sing it slow. The tap must match the word, or the magic is lost.
Offer your own hand sometimes and let {name} do the tapping.
Same song for weeks is perfect. Repetition is the feature, not the bug.
games.level_up: After the song, hold up one finger and ask: "How many is this?" Just once, just for fun.
games.level_down: Skip the numbers and tap the beat. Touch plus rhythm is the on-ramp.
games.bilingual_note: Songs in each home language both count. Pick the ones you actually remember.

games.title: How-Many Photo Hunt
games.goal: Notice and name tiny sets (one to three) in pictures and the world
materials: a picture book or your phone photos
script: Open a favorite book or your camera roll together.
Hunt for small groups: "Look! Two dogs!" Tap each one as you say it.
Keep it to one, two, and three. Small sets are the sweet spot.
Take turns. {name} points at something, you name the how-many.
When {name} names a number, agree warmly, even if the count is wild.
Three or four finds, then close the book while it's still fun.
games.level_up: Ask "how many?" before you name it, and give {name} first crack.
games.level_down: You do all the naming. Pointing along is full participation.
games.bilingual_note: Name the sets in either language, or both back to back. Two labels, one idea.

games.title: Bath Cup Pour and Talk
games.goal: Soak everyday bath play in number and amount words
script: Float two or three cups in the bath.
Narrate the pouring with number words: "One cup... two cups! Both cups are full."
Count the cups as you line them on the tub edge, tapping each one.
Ask for cups by number: "Hand me one cup, please!"
Whatever {name} hands over, say thank you and keep playing.
Let {name} dump everything at the end. Chaos is the closing ceremony.
games.level_up: Ask for two cups instead of one, once per bath.
games.level_down: Drop the requests and keep the narration. Hearing the words during play is the win.
games.bilingual_note: Bath talk works in any language you're comfortable in. Use the one that flows.

games.title: Two Eyes, One Nose
games.goal: Anchor one and two to the body the child knows best
script: During dressing or washing, tour the body with numbers.
Touch gently as you go: "Two eyes. One nose. Two ears. One belly!"
Make the twos a little song and the ones a little surprise.
Ask {name} to find the pairs on you: "Where are MY two ears?"
Finish with a count of ten toes, fast and silly. No quiz, ever.
games.level_up: Pause before the number: "How many noses?" Take any answer with a grin.
games.level_down: Just the touching and the words. The counting can stay yours for months.
games.bilingual_note: Body words plus number words in either language. Do the tour in both if you like.

games.title: Clap the Beat
games.goal: Feel small quantities as rhythm before naming them
script: Clap a tiny pattern and say it: "One, two!" Two claps, two words.
Invite a copy: "Your turn!" Any clapping back is a win.
Trade turns. Keep patterns at one, two, or three claps.
Add stomps or knee-slaps when claps get old.
Big finish: "THREE!" with three giant claps. Then done.
games.level_up: Hide a clap inside a cupped hand so {name} must listen, then ask for the same number back.
games.level_down: Clap together at the same time instead of taking turns. Shared beat first.
games.bilingual_note: Count the claps in either home language. The beat is the same in both.

games.title: Laundry Basket Toss
games.goal: One-at-a-time handling with a number word glued to each toss
script: Sorting laundry? Deputize {name} as the tosser.
Hand over socks one at a time: "One sock... in! Two socks... in!"
Say the number right as the item flies. Word and action together.
Cheer the landing, not the number: "What a throw!"
Occasionally hold up one item and name it: "ONE shirt. In it goes!"
Stop when the basket is full or the giggles run out.
games.level_up: Ask {name} to hand YOU one sock. Just one request per laundry day.
games.level_down: Toss together, hand over hand, with you saying the words.
games.bilingual_note: Narrate in whichever language you sort laundry in. Both languages count the same socks.

games.title: Snack Drop Song
games.goal: Make snack-serving a counted ritual the child can predict
script: Serve snack pieces one at a time into the bowl, counting each drop.
Use a sing-song voice: "Onnne... twooo... threee!" Plink, plink, plink.
Same tune every day. {name} will start humming the numbers with you.
Some days, stop mid-count and wait. Let {name} demand the next number.
The eating is the reward. No questions attached.
games.level_up: Ask: "One more or all done?" and honor the answer either way.
games.level_down: Count just to two, then pour the rest freely. Tiny ritual, zero pressure.
games.bilingual_note: Alternate languages by day if you like. Same tune, different words, same numbers.

games.title: Snack Plate Match
games.goal: Map small number words onto exact sets by matching plates
script: Put two plates on the table. Say: "One plate for you, one plate for me."
Put two snacks on your plate. Say: "Look, I have two. Can you make your plate match mine?"
Wait. Let {name} work it out. No counting for them, no hints.
Whatever lands on the plate, say: "Thank you! Let's check together. One... two."
If the plates match, celebrate the match, not the child: "Same! Both plates have two!"
Swap roles. Say: "Your turn. Put some on your plate, and I'll match you."
Play three or four rounds, then stop while it's still fun.
games.level_up: Once, playfully, make your plate hold three and ask for a match. If it flops, laugh and go back to two.
games.level_down: Drop to matching one snack, and let {name} be the one who builds the plate you copy.
games.bilingual_note: Play in either home language. Counting skill moves across languages with the child.

games.title: Feed the Bear, Free Play
games.goal: Practice giving exact tiny amounts with a very forgiving customer
script: Sit the bear down with its bowl. The bear is hungry and very polite.
Make the bear ask: "Can I have one block, please?"
Whatever {name} serves, the bear says thank you and pretend-munches loudly.
Mix tiny orders: one, then two, then one again.
Let {name} take a turn being the bear and giving YOU orders.
Serve the bear's dessert together, counting each piece into the bowl.
Bear falls asleep, game over. Always end with a full, happy bear.
games.level_up: The bear asks for one number bigger than {name}'s comfortable best, once, then orders easy things again.
games.level_down: The bear asks only for "one" and celebrates enormously every time.
games.bilingual_note: The bear happily speaks both home languages. Alternate its orders if you like.

games.title: Give-Me-One Errands
games.goal: Turn fetching into exact-amount practice, one request at a time
script: During any routine, place a tiny order: "Can you bring me one spoon?"
Whatever arrives, say thank you like it's exactly what you wanted.
Sprinkle three or four little errands through the day. That's plenty.
Keep most orders at one. Land on two only when one feels easy.
Sometimes reverse it: "Want one cracker or two?" and honor the answer.
games.level_up: Try "two" at the start of an errand you know {name} loves.
games.level_down: Point at the thing while you ask. Pointing plus the word is still the game.
games.bilingual_note: Give errands in either language. If two adults use different languages, even better.

games.title: One in Each Cup
games.goal: Build exactly-one-per-spot thinking with cups and treasures
script: Line up three or four cups upside-down-turned-up on the floor.
Say: "Every cup gets ONE treasure. Just one!"
Demonstrate the first cup slowly: "One for this cup."
Hand over the treasures and let {name} finish the row.
Check together by peeking in each cup: "One... one... one! Every cup has one!"
Dump and repeat. Dumping is half the fun.
games.level_up: Announce a doubles round: "Now every cup gets TWO!" Check the same way.
games.level_down: Use two cups only, and load them together, hand over hand.
games.bilingual_note: Run rounds in different home languages. "One" in each language lives in the same cup.

games.title: Stair Stop
games.goal: Make a number word control the body: climb exactly N and freeze
script: At the stairs, announce the mission: "Climb TWO steps and FREEZE!"
Count the climb together and freeze dramatically on the target step.
Hold the freeze for one giggle, then finish the stairs normally.
Alternate tiny missions: one step, two steps, back to one.
Let {name} give YOU a freeze number and catch you if you climb past it.
games.level_up: Stretch to three-step missions when two-step freezes feel easy and smug.
games.level_down: You climb and freeze while {name} watches and laughs, then climb together on your count.
games.bilingual_note: Call missions in either language. Freezing is universal.

games.title: Two-Tower
games.goal: Build sets of exactly two, over and over, until two feels solid
script: Declare tower law: "Every tower in this city is TWO blocks tall."
Build the first one, counting: "One... two. Done! City rules."
Hand over blocks and let {name} build more two-towers.
Inspect towers together, tapping each block: "One, two. Approved!"
A three-block tower? The inspector gasps, removes one, and everyone laughs.
Knock the whole city down at the end. Mandatory.
games.level_up: Change the law for one round: "Today, towers are THREE tall." Inspect the same way.
games.level_down: Build every tower together, your hand on theirs, counting slowly.
games.bilingual_note: Inspect in both home languages on different days. The law translates.

games.title: Shoe Pair Hunt
games.goal: Find twos everywhere: pairs are the world's favorite set
materials: the shoe pile by the door
script: Visit the shoe pile. Announce: "Shoes live in TWOS. Let's fix this mess!"
Hold up one shoe: "One shoe... where is its friend?"
When {name} finds the partner, line them up: "One, two. A pair!"
Count each finished pair with two happy taps.
March the pairs back to their spot, two by two.
Wrong partner? "These two don't match! Keep hunting." Matching is its own puzzle.
games.level_up: Count the pairs themselves at the end: "One pair, two pairs, three pairs!"
games.level_down: You find the partners; {name} does the two-tap on each pair.
games.bilingual_note: Hunt in either language. "A pair" has a word in both, and both mean two.

games.title: Two for the Truck
games.goal: Load exact small cargoes on request, then stretch to three
script: The truck pulls up. It has a job: "This truck needs TWO blocks!"
Let {name} load. Whatever the cargo, the truck drives off delighted.
Unload together at the other side, counting each block out.
New job, new number: two, then three, then back to two.
Give {name} the dispatcher job: they call the cargo number, you load it.
Load your cargo wrong sometimes. A dispatcher who catches you is learning.
games.level_up: Orders of four when threes ship smoothly.
games.level_down: Every job is "one big block," delivered with maximum truck noises.
games.bilingual_note: Dispatch in both home languages. Trucks are famously bilingual.

games.title: Napkin Setter
games.goal: Set the table with exact counts: real job, real sets
script: Before dinner, hire your setter: "We need three napkins tonight. One for each person!"
Count who's eating together, pointing at each chair.
Hand over the napkin stack and let {name} deal them out.
Check as a team: "Does every spot have one? Let's count. One... two... three!"
A missing spot or an extra napkin is a mystery to solve, not a mistake.
Repeat with spoons if dinner can wait two more minutes.
games.level_up: Add a guest and ask: "Now how many do we need?" Let the chairs answer.
games.level_down: Set two places only, and count the chairs together first, every time.
games.bilingual_note: Set the table in the language dinner happens in tonight. Rotate freely.

games.title: Berry Share
games.goal: Deal a snack into fair little sets and name what each person got
materials: a snack that comes in pieces
script: Two bowls, one pile of berries, one very important job.
Say: "One for you, one for me" and deal a few rounds together.
Stop and admire: "You have two! I have two! Same!"
Keep dealing and pause again at three each.
Let {name} run the deal while you narrate the numbers.
Eat the math. Best part.
games.level_up: Deal to three bowls when the third eater (bear included) shows up.
games.level_down: Deal just one berry each and marvel at the matching ones. Tiny sets, big deal.
games.bilingual_note: Deal in either language. Fair is fair in both.

games.title: Sock Match Factory
games.goal: Match and count tiny sets inside a chore you had to do anyway
script: Dump the clean socks in a glorious heap.
Pull one sock and hold it high: "One lonely sock! Find its twin!"
When the twin surfaces, press them together and count: "One, two. Twins!"
Stack finished pairs in a tower of twos.
Every few pairs, tap-count the stack together.
Retire when {name} starts wearing the socks as mittens. Natural endpoint.
games.level_up: Sort pairs by owner and count how many pairs each person gets.
games.level_down: You do the matching; {name} presses the twins together and gets the count said over them.
games.bilingual_note: Sort in whichever language laundry happens in. Twins translate.

games.title: Three Bears Picnic
games.goal: Serve exact sets of three and four across multiple hungry guests
script: Seat three bears (or whoever's available) around a picnic blanket.
Take orders: "This bear wants THREE berries. That one wants TWO."
Let {name} serve each guest their exact order.
The served bear counts its food aloud with your voice, tapping each piece.
A bear with the wrong amount just giggles and re-orders. No stern bears.
End with dessert for everyone: one cookie each, dealt by {name}.
Bears nap. Picnic over. Praise the waiter's hard work.
games.level_up: One bear orders FOUR, once per picnic, with great ceremony.
games.level_down: Two bears only, orders of one and two, and serve the first order together.
games.bilingual_note: Bears order in both home languages happily. Take orders in whichever flows today.

games.title: Parking Garage
games.goal: Count out exact fleets and park them spot by spot
script: You run the garage. Cars arrive in fleets.
Radio the order: "Three cars incoming! Park exactly three."
Let {name} drive the fleet in, one car per spot.
Inspect together, tapping the hood of each car: "One, two, three. Full house!"
Send fleets back out and call new numbers: four, then two, then three.
Swap jobs. {name} calls fleet sizes; you park them, sometimes wrong, to be caught.
games.level_up: Call a five-car fleet when fours park without a second thought.
games.level_down: Fleets of one and two, and park the first car together as the demo.
games.bilingual_note: Radio calls in either language. Cars obey both.

games.title: Grab Bag Check
games.goal: Grab a handful, then count to find out: checking is the game
script: Blocks go in the bag. Shake it importantly.
{name} grabs one handful and drops it on the floor.
Ask the magic question: "How many did you catch? Let's count and see!"
Count together, sliding each block aside as it's counted.
Announce the total like a game-show host: "FOUR! You caught four!"
Your turn to grab. Let {name} lead the counting of your haul.
games.level_up: Guess before counting: "I think three. Let's check!" Wrong guesses are delicious.
games.level_down: Grab tiny handfuls of one or two, and count hand over hand.
games.bilingual_note: Count hauls in either language, or once in each. Same blocks, same total.

games.title: Snack Factory
games.goal: Fill repeat orders of exact sizes: three, four, and the occasional five
materials: small cups or a muffin tin
script: Open the factory: cups are boxes, snacks are product, {name} is the packer.
Call the order: "Three crackers per box, please!"
Let {name} fill each box, counting or not, their choice.
Quality control is a team job: tap-count each box together before it ships.
Ship boxes to customers around the room (couch, bear, sibling).
Change the order size after a few boxes: "New order! FOUR per box!"
games.level_up: A special customer wants five. Big orders make the factory famous.
games.level_down: Boxes of two, and pack the first box together, tapping as you drop each piece.
games.bilingual_note: Take orders in both home languages. The factory exports everywhere.

games.title: Count-Out Helper
games.goal: Fetch exact amounts as real household help, counting on the way
script: Cooking or tidying? Place a real order: "I need FOUR potatoes for the pot."
Let {name} count them out from the bag, one by one.
Receive the delivery and recount together as you use them.
Thank your helper by name and by number: "Four potatoes! Dinner is saved."
One or two real errands a day beats ten drills.
games.level_up: Order five or six for jobs {name} loves, and let them double-check alone.
games.level_down: Order two, and count the fetch together on the way back.
games.bilingual_note: Order in whichever language the kitchen runs on tonight.

games.title: Red Light, Count Light
games.goal: Move exactly N steps on command: numbers steer the whole body
script: Stand across the room or yard from each other.
Call moves: "Take THREE giant steps!" {name} steps and counts aloud.
Freeze between moves. The freeze makes the counting matter.
Mix step sizes: two tiny steps, four giant steps, one jump.
First to reach the other side calls the next round.
Let {name} be the caller often. Calling numbers is harder than obeying them.
games.level_up: Five-step and six-step calls, and side-to-side steps for chaos.
games.level_down: Calls of one and two only, and step together while counting in chorus.
games.bilingual_note: Call moves in both home languages across rounds. Feet understand both.

games.title: Dot Card Peek
games.goal: See small amounts at a glance, then prove it by counting
materials: index cards with 1-6 big dots drawn on
script: Draw big dots on cards: one dot up to six dots. Messy is fine.
Flash a card for one second: "Peek! How many?"
Take any answer with delight, then flip the card back over for the count.
Count the dots together, touching each one. The count settles it.
Let {name} flash cards at you. Get some wrong. Be caught.
Five cards a round. Stop while it still feels like magic.
games.level_up: Shorter peeks, and ask "how do you know?" after confident answers.
games.level_down: Use only one-, two-, and three-dot cards, with long relaxed peeks.
games.bilingual_note: Peek and count in either language. Dots don't care.

games.title: High-Five Fingers
games.goal: Make five a friend: build it, break it, and find it on hands
script: Hold up your hand: "Five fingers! Count them with me."
Count and fold: fold each finger down as it's counted, then pop them all back up.
Show finger-numbers: "Show me three fingers! Now show me five!"
Play copycat: you flash a finger-number, {name} matches it on their hand.
High-five to finish. Obviously.
games.level_up: Ask for four fingers, then "one more" to reach five, and name what happened.
games.level_down: Count {name}'s fingers for them, folding gently, and stop at three sometimes.
games.bilingual_note: Fingers count identically in every language you speak. Rotate freely.

games.title: Four Corners Hunt
games.goal: Hunt for exact-size sets hiding in ordinary rooms
script: Announce the hunt: "Find me FOUR of something. Anything!"
Four spoons, four shoes, four crayons: any four wins.
Count the find together, tapping each item, to certify it.
Trade jobs: {name} calls a number, you hunt, they inspect your set.
Sneak in a wrong set on your turn and let the inspector catch it.
Three hunts each is a full game.
games.level_up: Hunt fives and sixes, or two sets at once: "Three forks AND two cups!"
games.level_down: Hunt twos and threes, and hunt as one team instead of trading jobs.
games.bilingual_note: Call hunts in either home language. The house is bilingual too.

games.title: Number Path Board Game
games.goal: March a token along a numbered path: the classic that moves the needle
script: Print the board. Each player picks a token and starts at 1.
Spin, then move that many spaces, SAYING EACH NUMBER YOU LAND ON: "Five, six!"
Say the numbers PRINTED on the spaces, never "one, two" for the moves. On 4, spin 2: say "five, six!"
Saying the numbers on the spaces is the whole engine. Gently insist on it.
Take turns. React big to every move, huge to none.
First to the end wins, and the loser demands a rematch. Grant it.
Play in short, frequent bursts across two weeks rather than one long slog.
games.level_up: Say the number you'll LAND on before moving. Prediction is the next gear.
games.level_down: Move one space per turn, reading each number together, no spinner race.
games.bilingual_note: Play rounds in each home language. The board's numbers belong to both.

games.title: Bear Restaurant
games.goal: Fill bigger exact orders under gentle restaurant pressure
script: The restaurant opens. {name} is chef. Bears are regulars with strong opinions.
Bears order in full sentences: "FIVE berries and TWO crackers, please."
Chef prepares the plate. The kitchen is calm; there is no rush.
Serve, then run the check together: tap-count each item on the plate.
A wrong order? The bear says: "Close! I ordered five. Can you fix my plate?" One fix, then eat.
Bears tip in hugs. Close the restaurant while the chef still loves the job.
games.level_up: Double orders (three AND three) or a six, for the ambitious chef.
games.level_down: Orders of two and three, and count out the first order together.
games.bilingual_note: Bears order in both home languages, sometimes in the same meal.

games.title: Guess, Then Count
games.goal: Estimate first, count to check: the scientist's two-step
script: Spot a pile: crackers, crayons, ducks in the bath.
Both players guess: "I say four. What do you say?"
Count together to settle it, moving each item as it's counted.
Crown the closer guess with a silly title: "Guess Champion of the Bathtub!"
Guess wrong a lot yourself. Being beatable is the point.
One pile per moment. It's a spice, not a meal.
games.level_up: Bigger piles (up to ten), and guesses BEFORE the pile settles.
games.level_down: Piles of two to four, and count the pile first, then "guess" together from memory.
games.bilingual_note: Guess in one language, check in the other. Double the number talk, same pile.

games.title: Count-Anything Club
games.goal: Count the world: any set, anywhere, membership permanent
script: Induct {name} into the club: members count interesting things wherever they go.
On walks and errands, spot countables: "Club alert! How many red cars?"
Count together or solo, member's choice. Totals get announced proudly.
Keep sets under ten so wins stay wins.
Trade discoveries: {name} finds you things to count too.
Two or three counts per outing. Then the club rests.
games.level_up: Count things that move or hide (birds, buses). Harder targets, same club.
games.level_down: Count only what sits still, and count in chorus together.
games.bilingual_note: The club counts in every language its members speak. Alternate proudly.

games.title: Snack Split
games.goal: Divide a snack fairly and prove the fairness by counting
materials: a snack that comes in pieces
script: Present the pile and the problem: "Eight crackers, two people. Make it fair."
Let {name} split it however they like. Dealing, grabbing, eyeballing: all legal.
Run the fairness check together: count each bowl aloud.
If it's uneven, hand the problem back: "Hmm, four and six. What now?"
Celebrate the fix like a solved mystery, then eat the evidence.
Add a third eater some days. Three-way fair is a whole new puzzle.
games.level_up: Start with an amount that can't split evenly and discover the leftover together.
games.level_down: Split four pieces between two bowls, dealing one at a time in chorus.
games.bilingual_note: Run the fairness check in either language. Fair is provable in both.

games.title: Hidden Counters
games.goal: Hold a counted set in mind after it disappears
script: Count four blocks together, slowly, touching each one.
Hide them under the cup with maximum drama.
Ask the impossible: "No peeking. How many are hiding?"
Any answer gets the same reply: "Let's look!" Lift and recount.
The reveal is the payoff. Gasp every time, even at wrong answers.
Swap roles. {name} hides, you "forget," they get to know better than you.
games.level_up: Hide five or six, or slide ONE more under without showing and recount the surprise.
games.level_down: Hide two or three, and whisper the count together while they're hidden.
games.bilingual_note: Hide in one language, reveal in the other. The blocks keep count either way.

games.title: Silly Count Patrol
games.goal: Catch counting mistakes: skipped items, double-counts, wrong totals
script: The puppet announces it is the BEST counter in the house.
The puppet counts five blocks... and skips one: "One, two, three, four. Four blocks!"
Wait. If {name} objects, act shocked and let them recount to prove it.
Mix in perfect counts so there's something real to certify.
Classic blunders: skipping, counting one block twice, ending on the wrong word.
The puppet thanks its supervisor and promises to do better. It won't.
games.level_up: Subtler errors, bigger sets, and ask: "What did puppet do wrong?"
games.level_down: Blatant errors on three blocks, and recount together in chorus after each catch.
games.bilingual_note: The puppet blunders in both home languages with equal confidence.

games.title: Calendar and Candles
games.goal: Count out meaningful numbers: ages, days, and candles
script: Draw a birthday cake together. Ask: "How old is Grandma's dog? Let's give it candles!"
Count out exactly that many candle-strokes onto the cake.
Draw cakes for family members, real ages optional, counted candles mandatory.
Recount each finished cake, tapping candles, to certify it.
Sing the song for the best cake. Blowing out paper candles is allowed.
Sneak one wrong cake in and let the pastry inspector catch you.
games.level_up: "Next birthday you'll be five. How many MORE candles will we need?"
games.level_down: Cakes with two and three candles, counted out together stroke by stroke.
games.bilingual_note: Sing and count in both home languages. Cakes are multilingual by nature.

games.title: One-More Bakery
games.goal: Feel what one more does to a set, over and over, deliciously
script: Open the bakery. Put three rolls (blocks) on the tray and count them together.
A customer calls: "Add ONE more roll!" Add it with a flourish.
Ask the baker: "NOW how many?" Count to check whatever they say.
Keep going: one more, one more. Watch the tray grow, count after each.
The magic to notice out loud: "One more makes it go three... FOUR!"
Then eat-down the inventory, one at a time, counting what's left if the baker's game.
games.level_up: Ask BEFORE counting: "Four rolls, one more coming. How many will there be?"
games.level_down: Stay at one-two-three, recounting from the start after each new roll.
games.bilingual_note: Take bakery orders in either home language. One more works the same in both.

games.title: Who Has More?
games.goal: Compare sets by counting, and let the count settle every argument
script: Grab two handfuls, one each. Drop them in two piles.
The big question: "Who has more? What do you think?"
Count both piles together, lining pieces up as you count.
Line the piles side by side, piece facing piece. Seeing the extra is the aha.
Announce the ruling: "Six beats four! The count has spoken."
Play again. Rig a tie sometimes and discover "the same!" together.
games.level_up: Ask HOW MANY more the winner has, and find the answer in the lined-up extras.
games.level_down: Compare piles of two versus four, where eyes alone can tell, then count to confirm.
games.bilingual_note: Hold court in either language. The count rules in both.

games.title: Next-Number Riddles
games.goal: Play with the count list itself: what comes after, what came before
script: In the car or a line, launch a riddle: "I'm thinking of the number after FOUR..."
Any answer gets a count-up check: "Let's climb: one, two, three, four... FIVE!"
Trade turns. {name}'s riddles for you can be as weird as they like.
Get some wrong on purpose. Being corrected by a four-year-old is premium content.
Three riddles per ride is the sweet spot.
games.level_up: Riddle downward: "What comes right BEFORE five?" Count up to check, and notice the trick.
games.level_down: Riddle only after numbers one and two, and always count up together from one.
games.bilingual_note: Riddle in both home languages. The count list climbs the same ladder in each.

games.title: Staircase Towers
games.goal: Build one, two, three, four as towers and see the ladder grow
script: Build a one-block tower. Next to it, a two-block tower. Say what you're doing.
Hand over the blocks: "What comes next in our staircase?"
Keep building: three, then four, each tower one block taller.
Walk your fingers up the staircase, counting each tower's height.
Stand back and admire it: "Every step is ONE more block!"
Demolition is the closing ceremony. Count the wreckage if anyone's still counting.
games.level_up: Build to six, or remove a middle tower and ask what's missing from the staircase.
games.level_down: Build just one-two-three together, counting each tower as a team.
games.bilingual_note: Build in one language today and the other tomorrow. Same staircase either way.

games.title: Number Neighbors
games.goal: Find each number's neighbors: the one before and the one after
script: Draw a row of little houses numbered 1 to 6. Sloppy houses welcome.
Pick a house: "Who lives next to house four?"
Walk fingers along the row to visit the neighbors: three on one side, five on the other.
Knock on doors out of order. Every knock gets a finger-walk check from house one.
Let {name} quiz you. Move into the wrong house occasionally.
End with a parade past every house, counting one to six.
games.level_up: Cover a house with your thumb and ask who's hiding between its neighbors.
games.level_down: Use houses one to three, and always finger-walk from house one together.
games.bilingual_note: Visit the neighbors in either home language. Same street, same houses.

games.title: One-Fewer Picnic
games.goal: Feel what taking one away does to a counted set
script: Lay out five snacks on the picnic plate and count them together.
The bear sneaks one while {name} watches. Dramatic munching.
Ask: "That sneaky bear! How many are left?"
Count to check whatever answer comes. The count is always the judge.
Keep going, one theft at a time, counting after each, down to zero.
Zero deserves a big finish: "NONE left! The bear ate the whole picnic!"
games.level_up: Ask BEFORE the recount: "Four now. Bear takes one. How many will be left?"
games.level_down: Start with three snacks, recounting slowly from the start after each theft.
games.bilingual_note: The bear steals snacks in both home languages. Count the losses in either.

games.title: The Long Count Walk
games.goal: Stretch the count list past ten with feet, not flashcards
script: On a walk, pick a target: "Let's count our steps to that tree!"
Count in step-rhythm together. When {name} stalls, feed the next number and roll on.
Celebrate the arrival total: "Nineteen steps! What a journey."
Pick targets of different sizes: near ones for solo counts, far ones for team counts.
The teens are the wobbliest part of the list. Walks smooth them out, trip by trip.
Two or three targets per walk. Then just walk.
games.level_up: Start counts from a running start: "Let's start at TEN. Ten, eleven..."
games.level_down: Count to five-step targets, in chorus, and let the rhythm carry the words.
games.bilingual_note: Count one target in each home language. The teens live in both lists.

games.title: Count the Pictures
games.goal: Share any picture book and land the count on its total
script: Snuggle up with any picture book. Favorites welcome.
On a page, find something there is more than one of: ducks, buttons, boots.
Count them out loud together, touching each one: "One, two..."
Land hard on the total: "Two ducks!" The last word is the prize.
Two or three counting pages make a full session. Story first, numbers second.
The same page every night? Wonderful. Repetition is the point.
games.level_up: When counting to three feels easy, hunt for pages with four, five, or six things.
games.level_down: You count, {name} touches. Land on the total together: "Two!"
games.bilingual_note: Count the pictures in either home language, always landing on the total.
